entries.0389e07acf6c4e46842e4977a87cf464de9348f0: <div sID="gen14886" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Eccl.3" sID="Eccl.3"/> <div eID="gen14886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14887" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14888" type="x-p"/> Solomon having shown the vanity of studies, pleasures, and business, and made it to appear that happiness is not to be found in the schools of the learned, nor in the gardens of Epicurus, nor upon the exchange, he proceeds, in this chapter, further to prove his doctrine, and the inference he had drawn from it, That therefore we should cheerfully content ourselves with, and make use of, what God has given us, by showing, I. The mutability of all human affairs, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. The immutability of the divine counsels concerning them and the unsearchableness of those counsels, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11-Eccl.3.15">ver. 11-15</reference>. III. The vanity of worldly honour and power, which are abused for the support of oppression and persecution if men be not governed by the fear of God in the use of them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">ver. 16</reference>. For a check to proud oppressors, and to show them their vanity, he reminds them, 1. That they will be called to account for it in the other world, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">ver. 17</reference>. 2. That their condition, in reference to this world (for of that he speaks), is no better than that of the beasts, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18-Eccl.3.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. And therefore he concludes that it is our wisdom to make use of what power we have for our own comfort, and not to oppress others with it.
entries.f4304c50d1c9e4fdf485f5d5a43de27c3685661f: <div eID="gen14888" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14887" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutability of Human Affairs.</title> <div sID="gen14889" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> To every <hi type="italic">thing there is</hi> a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: <hi type="super">2</hi> A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> planted; <hi type="super">3</hi> A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; <hi type="super">4</hi> A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; 5 A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; 6 A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; <hi type="super">7</hi> A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; <hi type="super">8</hi> A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. <hi type="super">9</hi> What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth? 10 I have seen the travail, which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it. <div eID="gen14889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14890" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to show, 1. That we live in a world of changes, that the several events of time, and conditions of human life, are vastly different from one another, and yet occur promiscuously, and we are continually passing and repassing between them, as in the revolutions of every day and every year. In the <hi type="italic">wheel of nature</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.6">Jam. iii. 6</reference>) sometimes one spoke is uppermost and by and by the contrary; there is a constant ebbing and flowing, waxing and waning; from one extreme to the other does the <hi type="italic">fashion of this world change,</hi> ever did, and ever will. 2. That every change concerning us, with the time and season of it, is unalterably fixed and determined by a supreme power; and we must take things as they come, for it is not in our power to change what is appointed for us. And this comes in here as a reason why, when we are in prosperity, we should by easy, and yet not secure—not to be secure because we live in a world of changes and therefore have no reason to say, <hi type="italic">To-morrow shall be as this day</hi> (the lowest valleys join to the highest mountains), and yet to be easy, and, as he had advised (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">ch. ii. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">to enjoy the good of our labour,</hi> in a humble dependence upon God and his providence, neither lifted up with hopes, nor cast down with fears, but with evenness of mind expecting every event. Here we have, <div eID="gen14890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14891" type="x-p"/> I. A general proposition laid down: <hi type="italic">To every thing there is a season,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Those things which seem most contrary the one to the other will, in the revolution of affairs, each take their turn and come into play. The day will give place to the night and the night again to the day. Is it summer? It will be winter. Is it winter? Stay a while, and it will be summer. Every purpose has its time. The clearest sky will be clouded, <hi type="italic">Post gaudia luctus—Joy succeeds sorrow;</hi> and the most clouded sky will clear up, <hi type="italic">Post nubila Phoebus—The sun will burst from behind the cloud.</hi> 2. Those things which to us seem most casual and contingent are, in the counsel and foreknowledge of God, punctually determined, and the very hour of them is fixed, and can neither be anticipated nor adjourned a moment. <div eID="gen14891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14892" type="x-p"/> II. The proof and illustration of it by the induction of particulars, twenty-eight in number, according to the days of the moon's revolution, which is always increasing or decreasing between its full and change. Some of these changes are purely the act of God, others depend more upon the will of man, but all are determined by the divine counsel. Every thing <hi type="italic">under heaven</hi> is thus changeable, but in heaven there is an unchangeable state, and an unchangeable counsel concerning these things. 1. There is <hi type="italic">a time to be born and a time to die.</hi> These are determined by the divine counsel; and, as we were born, so we must die, at the time appointed, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Acts xvii. 26</reference>. Some observe that here is <hi type="italic">a time to be born and a time to die,</hi> but no time to live; that is so short that it is not worth mentioning; as soon as we are born we begin to die. But, as there is <hi type="italic">a time to be born and a time to die,</hi> so there will be a time to rise again, a set time when those that lie in the grave shall be remembered, <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job xiv. 13</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">A time</hi> for God <hi type="italic">to plant</hi> a nation, as that of Israel in Canaan, <hi type="italic">and,</hi> in order to that, <hi type="italic">to pluck up</hi> the seven nations <hi type="italic">that were planted</hi> there, to make room for them; and at length there was a time when God spoke concerning Israel too, to <hi type="italic">pluck up and to destroy,</hi> when the measure of their iniquity was full, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jer. xviii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">9</reference>. There is <hi type="italic">a time</hi> for men <hi type="italic">to plant,</hi> a time of the year, a time of their lives; but, when <hi type="italic">that which was planted</hi> has grown fruitless and useless, it is <hi type="italic">time to pluck it up.</hi> 3. <hi type="italic">A time to kill,</hi> when the judgments of God are abroad in a land and lay all waste; but, when he returns in ways of mercy, then is <hi type="italic">a time to heal</hi> what <hi type="italic">he has torn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.2">Hos. vi. 1, 2</reference>), to comfort a people after the time that he has <hi type="italic">afflicted them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.15">Ps. xc. 15</reference>. There is a time when it is the wisdom of rulers to use severe methods, but there is a time when it is as much their wisdom to take a more gentle course, and to apply themselves to lenitives, not corrosives. 4. <hi type="italic">A time to break down</hi> a family, an estate, a kingdom, when it has ripened itself for destruction; but God will find <hi type="italic">a time,</hi> if they return and repent, to rebuild what he has broken down; there is <hi type="italic">a time,</hi> a set time, for the Lord <hi type="italic">to build up Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Ps. cii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.16">16</reference>. There is <hi type="italic">a time</hi> for men <hi type="italic">to break up</hi> house, and break off trade, and so <hi type="italic">to break down,</hi> which those that are busy in <hi type="italic">building up</hi> both must expect and prepare for. 5. <hi type="italic">A time</hi> when God's providence calls <hi type="italic">to weep and mourn,</hi> and when man's wisdom and grace will comply with the call, and will <hi type="italic">weep and mourn,</hi> as in times of common calamity and danger, and there it is very absurd to <hi type="italic">laugh, and dance,</hi> and make merry (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.13">Isa. xxii. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.10">Ezek. xxi. 10</reference>); but then, on the other hand, there is a time when God calls to cheerfulness, <hi type="italic">a time to laugh and dance,</hi> and then he expects we should <hi type="italic">serve him with joyfulness and gladness of heart.</hi> Observe, The time of mourning and weeping is put first, before that of laughter and dancing, for we must first <hi type="italic">sow in tears</hi> and then <hi type="italic">reap in joy.</hi> 6. <hi type="italic">A time to cast away stones,</hi> by breaking down and demolishing fortifications, when God gives peace in the borders, and there is no more occasion for them; but there is <hi type="italic">a time to gather stones together,</hi> for the making of strong-holds, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.5">v. 5</reference>. A time for old towers to fall, as that in Siloam (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Luke xii. 4</reference>), and for the temple itself to be so ruined as that <hi type="italic">not one stone should be left upon another;</hi> but also a time for towers and trophies too to be erected, when national affairs prosper. 7. <hi type="italic">A time to embrace</hi> a friend when we find him faithful, but <hi type="italic">a time to refrain from embracing</hi> when we find he is unfair or unfaithful, and that we have cause to suspect him; it is then our prudence to be shy and keep at a distance. It is commonly applied to conjugal embraces, and explained by <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.3-1Cor.7.5">1 Cor. vii. 3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joel ii. 16</reference>. 8. <hi type="italic">A time to get,</hi> get money, get preferment, get good bargains and a good interest, when opportunity smiles, a time when a wise man will <hi type="italic">seek</hi> (so the word is); when he is setting out in the world and has a growing family, when he is in his prime, when he prospers and has a run of business, then it is time for him to be busy and make hay when the sun shines. There is <hi type="italic">a time to get</hi> wisdom, and knowledge, and grace, when a man has a price put into his hand; but then let him expect there will come a time to spend, when all he has will be little enough to serve his turn. Nay, there will come <hi type="italic">a time to lose,</hi> when what has been soon got will be soon scattered and cannot be held fast. 9. <hi type="italic">A time to keep,</hi> when we have use for what we have got, and can keep it without running the hazard of a good conscience; but there may come <hi type="italic">a time to cast away,</hi> when love to God may oblige us to cast away what we have, because we must deny Christ and wrong our consciences if we keep it (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.37-Matt.10.38">Matt. x. 37, 38</reference>), and rather to make shipwreck of all than of the faith; nay, when love to ourselves may oblige us to cast it away, when it is for the saving of our lives, as it was when Jonah's mariners heaved their cargo into the sea. 10. <hi type="italic">A time to rend</hi> the garments, as upon occasion of some great grief, <hi type="italic">and a time to sew,</hi> them again, in token that the grief is over. A time to undo what we have done and a time to do again what we have undone. Jerome applies this to the rending of the Jewish church and the sewing and making up of the gospel church thereupon. 11. <hi type="italic">A time</hi> when it becomes us, and is our wisdom and duty, <hi type="italic">to keep silence,</hi> when it is an <hi type="italic">evil time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amos v. 13</reference>), when our speaking would be the <hi type="italic">casting of pearl before swine,</hi> or when we are in danger of speaking amiss (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.2">Ps. xxxix. 2</reference>); but there is also <hi type="italic">a time to speak</hi> for the glory of God and the edification of others, when silence would be the betraying of a righteous cause, and when with the mouth confession is to be made to salvation; and it is a great part of Christian prudence to know when to speak and when to hold our peace. 12. <hi type="italic">A time to love,</hi> and to show ourselves friendly, to be free and cheerful, and it is a pleasant time; but there may come <hi type="italic">a time to hate,</hi> when we shall see cause to break off all familiarity with some that we have been fond of, and to be upon the reserve, as having found reason for a suspicion, which love is loth to admit. 13. <hi type="italic">A time of war,</hi> when God draws the sword for judgment and gives it commission to devour, when men draw the sword for justice and the maintaining of their rights, when there is in the nations a disposition to war; but we may hope for <hi type="italic">a time of peace,</hi> when the sword of the Lord shall be sheathed and he shall <hi type="italic">make wars to cease</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">Ps. xlvi. 9</reference>), when the end of the war is obtained, and when there is on all sides a disposition to peace. War shall not last always, nor is there any peace to be called lasting on this side the everlasting peace. Thus in all these changes God has set the one over-against the other, that we may <hi type="italic">rejoice as though we rejoiced not and weep as though we wept not.</hi> <div eID="gen14892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14893" type="x-p"/> III. The inferences drawn from this observation. If our present state be subject to such vicissitude, 1. Then we must not expect our portion in it, for the good things of it are of no certainty, no continuance (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">What profit has he that works?</hi> What can a man promise himself from planting and building, when that which he thinks is brought to perfection may so soon, and will so surely, be plucked up and broken down? All our pains and care will not alter either the mutable nature of the things themselves or the immutable counsel of God concerning them. 2. Then we must look upon ourselves as upon our probation in it. There is indeed no profit <hi type="italic">in that wherein we labour;</hi> the thing itself, when we have it, will do us little good; but, if we make a right use of the disposals of Providence about it, there will be profit in that (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have seen the travail which God has given to the sons of men,</hi> not to make up a happiness by it, but <hi type="italic">to be exercised in it,</hi> to have various graces exercised by the variety of events, to have their dependence upon God tried by every change, and to be trained up to it, and taught both <hi type="italic">how to want and how to abound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Phil. iv. 12</reference>. Note, (1.) There is a great deal of toil and trouble to be seen among the children of men. Labour and sorrow fill the world. (2.) This toil and this trouble are what God has allotted us. He never intended this world for our rest, and therefore never appointed us to take our ease in it. (3.) To many it proves a gift. God gives it to men, as the physician gives a medicine to his patient, to do him good. This travail is given to us to make us weary of the world and desirous of the remaining rest. It is given to us that we may be kept in action, and may always have something to do; for we were none of us sent into the world to be idle. Every change cuts us out some new work, which we should be more solicitous about, than about the event.
entries.80facc60e63e16273b936f6c1297df82bcfe846c: <div eID="gen14893" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutability of Human Affairs.</title> <div sID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> He hath made every <hi type="italic">thing</hi> beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end. <hi type="super">12</hi> I know that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no good in them, but for <hi type="italic">a man</hi> to rejoice, and to do good in his life. <hi type="super">13</hi> And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gift of God. <hi type="super">14</hi> I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that <hi type="italic">men</hi> should fear before him. <hi type="super">15</hi> That which hath been is now; and that which is to be hath already been; and God requireth that which is past. <div eID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14895" type="x-p"/> We have seen what changes there are in the world, and must not expect to find the world more sure to us than it has been to others. Now here Solomon shows the hand of God in all those changes; it is he that has made every creature to be that to us which it is, and therefore we must have our eye always upon him. <div eID="gen14895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14896" type="x-p"/> I. We must make the best of <hi type="italic">that which is,</hi> and must believe it best for the present, and accommodate ourselves to it: <hi type="italic">He has made every thing beautiful in his time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">v. 11</reference>), and therefore, while its time lasts, we must be reconciled to it: nay, we must please ourselves with the beauty of it. Note, 1. Every thing is as God has made it; it is really as he appointed it to be, not as it appears to us. 2. That which to us seems most unpleasant is yet, in its proper time, altogether becoming. Cold is as becoming in winter as heat in summer; and the night, in its turn, is a black beauty, as the day, in its turn, is a bright one. 3. There is a wonderful harmony in the divine Providence and all its disposals, so that the events of it, when they come to be considered in their relations and tendencies, together with the seasons of them, will appear very beautiful, to the glory of God and the comfort of those that trust in him. Though we see not the complete beauty of Providence, yet we shall see it, and a glorious sight it will be, when the mystery of God shall be finished. Then every thing shall appear to have been done in the most proper time and it will be the wonder of eternity, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deut. xxxii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.18">Ezek. i. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen14896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14897" type="x-p"/> II. We must wait with patience for the full discovery of that which to us seems intricate and perplexed, acknowledging that we <hi type="italic">cannot find out the work that God makes from the beginning to the end,</hi> and therefore must judge nothing before the time. We are to believe that God has made all beautiful. Every thing is done well, as in creation, so in providence, and we shall see it when the end comes, but till then we are incompetent judges of it. While the picture is in drawing, and the house in building, we see not the beauty of either; but when the artist has put his last hand to them, and given them their finishing strokes, then all appears very good. We see but the middle of God's works, not from the beginning of them (then we should see how admirably the plan was laid in the divine counsels), nor to the end of them, which crowns the action (then we should see the product to be glorious), but we must wait till the veil be rent, and not arraign God's proceedings nor pretend to pass judgment on them. <hi type="italic">Secret things belong not to us.</hi> Those words, <hi type="italic">He has set the world in their hearts,</hi> are differently understood. 1. Some make them to be a reason why we may know more of God's works than we do; so Mr. Pemble: "God has not left himself without witness of his righteous, equal, and beautiful ordering of things, but has set it forth, to be observed in the book of <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> and this he has <hi type="italic">set in men's hearts,</hi> given man a large desire, and a power, in good measure, to comprehend and understand the history of nature, with the course of human affairs, so that, if men did but give themselves to the exact observation of things, they might in most of them perceive an admirable order and contrivance." 2. Others make them to be a reason why we do not know so much of God's works as we might; so bishop Reynolds: "We have the world so much in our hearts, are so taken up with thoughts and cares of worldly things, and are so exercised in our travail concerning them, that we have neither time nor spirit to eye God's hand in them." The world has not only gained possession of the heart, but has formed prejudices there against the beauty of God's works. <div eID="gen14897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14898" type="x-p"/> III. We must be pleased with our lot in this world, and cheerfully acquiesce in the will of God concerning us, and accommodate ourselves to it. <hi type="italic">There is no</hi> certain, lasting, <hi type="italic">good in</hi> these things; what good there is in them we are here told, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12-Eccl.3.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. We must make a good use of them, 1. For the benefit of others. All the <hi type="italic">good</hi> there is <hi type="italic">in them</hi> is <hi type="italic">to do good</hi> with them, to our families, to our neighbours, to the poor, to the public, to its civil and religious interests. What have we our beings, capacities, and estates for, but to be some way serviceable to our generation? We mistake if we think we were born for ourselves. No; it is our business <hi type="italic">to do good;</hi> it is in doing good that there is the truest pleasure, and what is so laid out is best laid up and will turn to the best account. Observe, It is <hi type="italic">to do good in this life,</hi> which is short and uncertain; we have but a little time to be doing good in, and therefore had need to redeem time. It is <hi type="italic">in this life,</hi> where we are in a state of trial and probation for another life. Every man's life is his opportunity of doing that which will make for him in eternity. 2. For our own comfort. Let us make ourselves easy, <hi type="italic">rejoice, and enjoy the good of our labour,</hi> as <hi type="italic">it is the gift of God,</hi> and so enjoy God in it, and taste his love, return him thanks, and make him the centre of our joy, <hi type="italic">eat and drink</hi> to his glory, and <hi type="italic">serve him with joyfulness of heart, in the abundance of all things.</hi> If all things in this world be so uncertain, it is a foolish thing for men sordidly to spare for the present, that they may hoard up all for hereafter; it is better to live cheerfully and usefully upon what we have, and let to-morrow <hi type="italic">take thought for the things of itself.</hi> Grace and wisdom to do this <hi type="italic">is the gift of God,</hi> and it is a good gift, which crowns the gifts of his providential bounty. <div eID="gen14898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14899" type="x-p"/> IV. We must be entirely satisfied in all the disposals of the divine Providence, both as to personal and public concerns, and bring our minds to them, because God, in all, performs the thing that is appointed for us, acts according to the counsel of his will; and we are here told, 1. That that counsel cannot be altered, and therefore it is our wisdom to make a virtue of necessity, by submitting to it. It must be as God wills: <hi type="italic">I know</hi> (and every one knows it that knows any thing of God) <hi type="italic">that whatsoever God does it shall be for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">He is in one mind, and who can turn him?</hi> His measures are never broken, nor is he ever put upon new counsels, but what he has purposed shall be effected, and all the world cannot defeat nor disannul it. It behoves us therefore to say, "Let it be as God wills," for, how cross soever it may be to our designs and interests, God's will is his wisdom. 2. That that counsel needs not to be altered, for there is nothing amiss in it, nothing that can be amended. If we could see it altogether at one view, we should see it so perfect that <hi type="italic">nothing can be put to it,</hi> for there is no deficiency in it, <hi type="italic">nor any thing taken from it,</hi> for there is nothing in it unnecessary, or that can be spared. As the word of God, so the works of God are every one of them perfect in its kind, and it is presumption for us either to add to them or to diminish from them, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">Deut. iv. 2</reference>. It is therefore as much our interest, as our duty, to bring our wills to the will of God. <div eID="gen14899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14900" type="x-p"/> V. We must study to answer God's end in all his providences, which is in general to make us religious. <hi type="italic">God does</hi> all <hi type="italic">that men should fear before him,</hi> to convince them that there is a God above them that has a sovereign dominion over them, at whose disposal they are and all their ways, and in whose hands their times are and all events concerning them, and that therefore they ought to have their eyes ever towards him, to worship and adore him, to acknowledge him in all their ways, to be careful in every thing to please him, and afraid of offending him in any thing. God thus changes his disposals, and yet is unchangeable in his counsels, not to perplex us, much less to drive us to despair, but to teach us our duty to him and engage us to do it. That which God designs in the government of the world is the support and advancement of religion among men. <div eID="gen14900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14901" type="x-p"/> VI. Whatever changes we see or feel in this world, we must acknowledge the inviolable steadiness of God's government. The sun rises and sets, the moon increases and decreases, and yet both are where they were, and their revolutions are in the same method from the beginning according to <hi type="italic">the ordinances of heaven;</hi> so it is with the events of Providence (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">That which has been is now.</hi> God has not of late begun to use this method. No; things were always as mutable and uncertain as they are now, and so they will be: <hi type="italic">That which is to be has already been;</hi> and therefore we speak inconsiderately when we say, "Surely the world was never so bad as it is now," or "None ever met with such disappointments as we meet with," or "The times will never mend;" they may mend with us, and after a time to mourn there may come a time to rejoice, but that will still be liable to the common character, to the common fate. The world, as it has been, is and will be constant in inconstancy; for <hi type="italic">God requires that which is past,</hi> that is, repeats what he has formerly done and deals with us no otherwise than as he has used to deal with good men; and <hi type="italic">shall the earth be forsaken for us, or the rock removed out of his place?</hi> There has no change befallen us, nor any temptation by it overtaken us, <hi type="italic">but such as is common to men.</hi> Let us not be proud and secure in prosperity, for God may recall a past trouble, and order that to seize us and spoil our mirth (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Ps. xxx. 7</reference>); nor let us despond in adversity, for God may call back the comforts that are past, as he did to Job. We may apply this to our past actions, and our behaviour under the changes that have affected us. God will call us to account for <hi type="italic">that which is past;</hi> and therefore, when we enter into a new condition, we should judge ourselves for our sins in our former condition, prosperous or afflicted.
entries.261806c55058c2eec3fe3e34b1263efb8ed28c99: <div eID="gen14901" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Immutability of God's Counsel; The Extent of Mortality.</title> <div sID="gen14902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And moreover I saw under the sun the place of judgment, <hi type="italic">that</hi> wickedness <hi type="italic">was</hi> there; and the place of righteousness, <hi type="italic">that</hi> iniquity <hi type="italic">was</hi> there. <hi type="super">17</hi> I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a time there for every purpose and for every work. <hi type="super">18</hi> I said in mine heart concerning the estate of the sons of men, that God might manifest them, and that they might see that they themselves are beasts. <hi type="super">19</hi> For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity. <hi type="super">20</hi> All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. <hi type="super">21</hi> Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth? <hi type="super">22</hi> Wherefore I perceive that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that <hi type="italic">is</hi> his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him? <div eID="gen14902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14903" type="x-p"/> Solomon is still showing that every thing in this world, without piety and the fear of God, is vanity. Take away religion, and there is nothing valuable among men, nothing for the sake of which a wise man would think it worth while to live in this world. In these verses he shows that power (than which there is nothing men are more ambitious of) and life itself (than which there is nothing men are more fond, more jealous of) are nothing without the fear of God. <div eID="gen14903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14904" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the vanity of man as mighty, man in his best estate, man upon the throne, where his authority is submitted to, man upon the judgment-seat, where his wisdom and justice are appealed to, and where, if he be governed by the laws of religion, he is God's vicegerent; nay, he is of those to whom it is said, <hi type="italic">You are gods;</hi> but without the fear of God it <hi type="italic">is vanity,</hi> for, set that aside, and, <div eID="gen14904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14905" type="x-p"/> 1. The judge will not judge aright, will not use his power well, but will abuse it; instead of doing good with it he will do hurt with it, and then it is not only vanity, but a lie, a cheat to himself and to all about him, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">v. 16</reference>. Solomon perceived, by what he had read of former times, what he heard of other countries, and what he had seen in some corrupt judges, even in the land of Israel, notwithstanding all his care to prefer good men, that there was <hi type="italic">wickedness in the place of judgment.</hi> It is not so above the sun: far be it from God that he should do iniquity, or pervert justice. But <hi type="italic">under the sun</hi> it is often found that that which should be the refuge, proves the prison, of oppressed innocency. <hi type="italic">Man being in honour, and not understanding</hi> what he ought to do, <hi type="italic">becomes like the beasts that perish,</hi> like the beasts of prey, even the most ravenous, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">Ps. xlix. 20</reference>. Not only from the persons that sat in judgment, but even <hi type="italic">in the places</hi> where judgment was, in pretence, administered, and righteousness was expected, <hi type="italic">there was iniquity;</hi> men met with the greatest wrongs in those courts to which they fled for justice. This is <hi type="italic">vanity and vexation;</hi> for, (1.) It would have been better for the people to have had no judges than to have had such. (2.) It would have been better for the judges to have had no power than to have had it and used it to such ill purposes; and so they will say another day. <div eID="gen14905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14906" type="x-p"/> 2. The judge will himself be judged for not judging aright. When Solomon saw how judgment was perverted among men he looked up to God the Judge, and looked forward to the day of his judgment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I said in my heart</hi> that this unrighteous judgment is not so conclusive as both sides take it to be, for there will be a review of the judgment; <hi type="italic">God shall judge</hi> between <hi type="italic">the righteous and the wicked,</hi> shall judge for the righteous and plead their cause, though now it is run down, and judge against the wicked and reckon with them for all their <hi type="italic">unrighteous decrees</hi> and the <hi type="italic">grievousness which they have prescribed,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1">Isa. x. 1</reference>. With an eye of faith we may see, not only the period, but the punishment of the pride and cruelty of oppressors (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.7">Ps. xcii. 7</reference>), and it is an unspeakable comfort to the oppressed that their cause will be heard over again. Let them therefore wait with patience, for there is another <hi type="italic">Judge</hi> that <hi type="italic">stands before the door.</hi> And, though the day of affliction may last long, yet <hi type="italic">there is a time,</hi> a set time, for the examination of <hi type="italic">every purpose, and every work</hi> done under the sun. Men have their day now, but God's day is coming, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. With God <hi type="italic">there is a time</hi> for the re-hearing of causes, redressing of grievances, and reversing of unjust decrees, though as yet we see it not here, <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job xxiv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen14906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14907" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the vanity of man as mortal. He now comes to speak more generally <hi type="italic">concerning the estate of the sons of men</hi> in this world, their life and being on earth, and shows that their reason, without religion and the fear of God, advances them but little above the beasts. Now observe, <div eID="gen14907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14908" type="x-p"/> 1. What he aims at in this account of man's estate. (1.) That God may be honoured, may be justified, may be glorified—<hi type="italic">that they might clear God</hi> (so the margin reads it), that if men have an uneasy life in this world, full of vanity and vexation, they may thank themselves and lay no blame on God; let them clear him, and not say that he made this world to be man's prison and life to be his penance; no, God made man, in respect both of honour and comfort, <hi type="italic">little lower than the angels;</hi> if he be mean and miserable, it is his own fault. Or, <hi type="italic">that God</hi> (that is, the world of God) <hi type="italic">might manifest them,</hi> and discover them to themselves, and so appear to be <hi type="italic">quick and powerful,</hi> and a judge of men's characters; and we may be made sensible how open we lie to God's knowledge and judgment. (2.) That men may be humbled, may be vilified, may be mortified—<hi type="italic">that they might see that they themselves are beasts.</hi> It is no easy matter to convince proud men that <hi type="italic">they are but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), much more to convince bad men <hi type="italic">that they are beasts,</hi> that, being destitute of religion, they are as <hi type="italic">the beasts that perish,</hi> as <hi type="italic">the horse and the mule that have no understanding.</hi> Proud oppressors are as beasts, as <hi type="italic">roaring lions and ranging bears.</hi> Nay, every man that minds his body only, and not his soul, makes himself no better than a brute, and must wish, at least, to die like one. <div eID="gen14908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14909" type="x-p"/> 2. The manner in which he verifies this account. That which he undertakes to prove is that a worldly, carnal, earthly-minded <hi type="italic">man, has no preeminence above the beast, for all</hi> that which he sets his heart upon, places his confidence, and expects a happiness in, <hi type="italic">is vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">v. 19</reference>. Some make this to be the language of an atheist, who justifies himself in his iniquity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">v. 16</reference>) and evades the argument taken from the judgment to come (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">v. 17</reference>) by pleading that there is not another life after this, but that when man dies there is an end of him, and therefore while he lives he may live as he lists; but others rather think Solomon here speaks as he himself thinks, and that it is to be understood in the same sense with that of his father (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Like sheep they are laid in the grave,</hi> and that he intends to show the vanity of this world's wealth and honours "By the equal condition in mere outward respects (as bishop Reynolds expounds it) between men and beasts," (1.) The events concerning both seem much alike (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">That which befals the sons of men</hi> is no other than that which <hi type="italic">befals beasts;</hi> a great deal of knowledge of human bodies is gained by the anatomy of the bodies of brutes. When the deluge swept away the old world the beasts perished with mankind. Horses and men are killed in battle with the same weapons of war. (2.) The end of both, to an eye of sense, seems alike too: <hi type="italic">They have all one breath,</hi> and breathe in the same air, and it is the general description of both that <hi type="italic">in their nostrils is the breath of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.22">Gen. vii. 22</reference>), and therefore, <hi type="italic">as the one dies, so dies the other;</hi> in their expiring there is no visible difference, but death makes much the same change with a beast that it does with a man. [1.] As to their bodies, the change is altogether the same, except the different respects that are paid to them by the survivors. Let a man be <hi type="italic">buried with the burial of an ass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jer. xxii. 19</reference>) and what pre&#235;minence then has he <hi type="italic">above a beast?</hi> The touch of the dead body of a man, by the law of Moses, contracted a greater ceremonial pollution than the touch of the carcase even of an unclean beast or fowl. And Solomon here observes that <hi type="italic">all go unto one place;</hi> the dead bodies of men and beasts putrefy alike; <hi type="italic">all are of the dust,</hi> in their original, for we see <hi type="italic">all turn to dust again</hi> in their corruption. What little reason then have we to be proud of our bodies, or any bodily accomplishments, when they must not only be reduced to the earth very shortly, but must be so in common with the beasts, and we must mingle our dust with theirs! [2.] As to their spirits there is indeed a vast difference, but not a visible one, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">v. 21</reference>. It is certain that <hi type="italic">the spirit of</hi> the sons of men at death is ascending; it <hi type="italic">goes upwards</hi> to the Father of spirits, who made it, to the world of spirits to which it is allied; it dies not with the body, but <hi type="italic">is redeemed from the power of the grave,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Ps. xlix. 15</reference>. It <hi type="italic">goes upwards</hi> to be judged and determined to an unchangeable state. It is certain that <hi type="italic">the spirit of the beast goes downwards to the earth;</hi> it dies with the body; it perishes and is gone at death. The soul of a beast is, at death, like a candle blown out—there is an end of it; whereas the soul of a man is then like a candle taken out of a dark lantern, which leaves the lantern useless indeed, but does itself shine brighter. This great difference there is between the spirits of men and beasts; and a good reason it is why men should <hi type="italic">set their affections on things above,</hi> and lift up their souls to those things, not suffering them, as if they were the souls of brutes, to cleave to this earth. But <hi type="italic">who knows</hi> this difference? We cannot see the ascent of the one and the descent of the other with our bodily eyes; and therefore those that live by sense, as all carnal sensualists do, that <hi type="italic">walk in the sight of their eyes</hi> and will not admit any other discoveries, by their own rule of judgment have no <hi type="italic">pre&#235;minence above the beasts. Who knows,</hi> that is, who considers this? <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>. Very few. Were it better considered, the world would be every way better; but most men live as if they were to be here always, or as if when they die there were an end of them; and it is not strange that those live like beasts who think they shall die like beasts, but on such the noble faculties of reason are perfectly lost and thrown away. <div eID="gen14909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14910" type="x-p"/> 3. An inference drawn from it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is nothing better,</hi> as to this world, nothing better to be had out of our wealth and honour, <hi type="italic">than that a man should rejoice in his own works,</hi> that is, (1.) Keep a clear conscience, and never admit <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> into <hi type="italic">the place of righteousness. Let every man prove his own work,</hi> and approve himself to God in it, <hi type="italic">so shall he have rejoicing in himself alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Gal. vi. 4</reference>. Let him not get nor keep any thing but what he can rejoice in. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>. (2.) Live a cheerful life. If God have prospered the work of our hands unto us, let us rejoice in it, and take the comfort of it, and not make it a burden to ourselves and leave others the joy of it; <hi type="italic">for that is our portion,</hi> not the portion of our souls (miserable are those that have their portion in this life, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>, and fools are those that choose it and take up with it, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Luke xii. 19</reference>), but it is the portion of the body; that only which we enjoy is ours out of this world; it is taking what is to be had and making the best of it, and the reason is because none can give us a sight of <hi type="italic">what shall be after us,</hi> either who shall have our estates or what use they will make of them. When we are gone it is likely we shall not see what is after us; there is no correspondence that we know of between the other world and this, <reference osisRef="Job.14.21">Job xiv. 21</reference>. Those in the other world will be wholly taken up with that world, so that they will not care for seeing what is done in this; and while we are here we cannot foresee <hi type="italic">what shall be after us,</hi> either as to our families or the public. <hi type="italic">It is not for us to know the times and seasons</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall be after</hi> us, which, as it should be a restraint to our cares about this world, so it should be a reason for our concern about another. Since death is a final farewell to this life, let us look before us to another life.  <chapter eID="Eccl.3"/> <div eID="gen14910" type="x-p"/>

entries.3ef70408632023aed62dd6fa1f9754a9ed17dd03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8020"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:1-22</reference>.<div eID="gen12440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> Earthly pursuits are no doubt lawful in their proper time and order (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.8">Ec 3:1-8</reference>), but unprofitable when out of time and place; as for instance, when pursued as the solid and chief good (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.9">Ec 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.10">10</reference>); whereas God makes everything beautiful in its season, which man obscurely comprehends (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>). God allows man to enjoy moderately and virtuously His earthly gifts (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">13</reference>). What consoles us amidst the instability of earthly blessings is, God's counsels are immutable (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Ec 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8020"/>1. Man has his appointed cycle of seasons and vicissitudes, as the sun, wind, and water (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5-Eccl.1.7">Ec 1:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen12442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purpose--</hi>as there is a fixed "season" in God's "purposes" (for example, He has fixed the "time" when man is "to be born," and "to die," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.2">Ec 3:2</reference>), so there is a lawful "time" for man to carry out his "purposes" and inclinations. God does not condemn, but approves of, the use of earthly blessings (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>); it is the abuse that He condemns, the making them the chief end (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">1Co 7:31</reference>). The earth, without human desires, love, taste, joy, sorrow, would be a dreary waste, without water; but, on the other hand, the misplacing and excess of them, as of a flood, need control. Reason and revelation are given to control them. <div eID="gen12443" type="x-p"/>
entries.0903253583ec697ed4c9b6132a1fda20b10fb71b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8021"/><div sID="gen12444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8021"/><hi type="bold">2. time to die--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.31.15">Psa 31:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">He 9:27</reference>).<div eID="gen12444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plant--</hi>A man can no more reverse the times and order of "planting," and of "digging up," and transplanting, than he can alter the times fixed for his "birth" and "death." To try to "plant" out of season is vanity, however good in season; so to make earthly things the chief end is vanity, however good they be in order and season. Gill takes it, not so well, figuratively (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jr 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Am 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.15.13">Mt 15:13</reference>). <div eID="gen12445" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b313009e9fd26d0340bd18a6e442059add5d6a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8022"/><div sID="gen12446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8022"/><hi type="bold">3. time to kill--</hi>namely, judicially, criminals; or, in wars of self-defense; not in malice. Out of this time and order, killing is murder.<div eID="gen12446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to heal--</hi>God has His times for "healing" (literally, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.5">Is 38:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">21</reference>; figuratively, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">De 32:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Ho 6:1</reference>; spiritually, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.3">Psa 147:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>). To heal spiritually, before the sinner feels his wound, would be "out of time," and so injurious.<div eID="gen12447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time to break down--</hi>cities, as Jerusalem, by Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen12448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">build up--</hi>as Jerusalem, in the time of Zerubbabel; spiritually (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>), "the set time" (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.16">Psa 102:13-16</reference>). <div eID="gen12449" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1250f2d8dcb001c85167b96c4bb8839b716e511: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8023"/><div sID="gen12450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8023"/><hi type="bold">4. mourn--</hi>namely, for the dead (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.2">Ge 23:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dance--</hi>as David before the ark (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.14">2Sa 6:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.11">Psa 30:11</reference>); spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">Mt 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.21">Lu 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.25">15:25</reference>). The Pharisees, by requiring sadness out of time, erred seriously. <div eID="gen12451" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7a8d97734547501aa63d9af924200f83ba8b411: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8024"/><div sID="gen12452" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8024"/><hi type="bold">5. cast away stones--</hi>as out of a garden or vineyard (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather--</hi>for building; figuratively, the Gentiles, once castaway stones, were in due time made parts of the spiritual building (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>, 20), and children of Abraham (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.9">Mt 3:9</reference>); so the restored Jews hereafter (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.16">Zec 9:16</reference>).<div eID="gen12453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">refrain ... embracing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen12454" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a75ab5984243300afb02e64c1496bb69de1aa62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8025"/><div sID="gen12455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8025"/><hi type="bold">6. time to get--</hi>for example, to gain honestly a livelihood (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">Ep 4:23</reference>).<div eID="gen12455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lose--</hi>When God wills losses to us, then is our time to be content.<div eID="gen12456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep--</hi>not to give to the idle beggar (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">2Th 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast away--</hi>in charity (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pr 11:24</reference>); or to part with the dearest object, rather than the soul (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.43">Mr 9:43</reference>). To be careful is right in its place, but not when it comes between us and Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.40-Luke.10.42">Lu 10:40-42</reference>). <div eID="gen12458" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9a7aa2618a767ead0ffac97a8345338e2239137: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8026"/><div sID="gen12459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8026"/><hi type="bold">7. rend--</hi>garments, in mourning (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joe 2:13</reference>); figuratively, nations, as Israel from Judah, already foretold, in Solomon's time (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.30">1Ki 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.31">31</reference>), to be "sewed" together hereafter (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.15">Eze 37:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen12459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">silence--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Am 5:13</reference>), in a national calamity, or that of a friend (<reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>); also not to murmur under God's visitation (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Le 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Psa 39:1</reference>, 2, 9). <div eID="gen12460" type="x-p"/>
entries.a741411d30be540890ae8f2cbf64f563742f4ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8027"/><div sID="gen12461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8027"/><hi type="bold">8. hate--</hi>for example, sin, lusts (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Lu 14:26</reference>); that is, to love God so much more as to seem in comparison to hate "father or mother," when coming between us and God.<div eID="gen12461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a time of war ... peace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.14.31">Lu 14:31</reference>). <div eID="gen12462" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b5b02dba0365735f768d0c6ae8d3a3f8d6e507b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8028"/><div sID="gen12463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8028"/>9. But these earthly pursuits, while lawful in their season, are "unprofitable" when made by man, what God never intended them to be, the chief good. Solomon had tried to create an artificial forced joy, at times when he ought rather to have been serious; the result, therefore, of his labor to be happy, out of God's order, was disappointment. "A time to plant" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.2">Ec 3:2</reference>) refers to his planting (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.5">Ec 2:5</reference>); "laugh" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.4">Ec 3:4</reference>), to <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ec 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>; "his mirth," "laughter"; "build up," "gather stones" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.3">Ec 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.5">5</reference>), to his "building" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.4">Ec 2:4</reference>); "embrace," "love," to his "princess" (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Ec 2:8</reference>); "get" (perhaps also "gather," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.5">Ec 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.6">6</reference>), to his "gathering" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Ec 2:8</reference>). All these were of "no profit," because not in God's time and order of bestowing happiness. <div eID="gen12463" type="x-p"/>
entries.1836b3cbd43c00776f6aa1f5ca9ed1e8de907e28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8029"/><div sID="gen12464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8029"/>10. (See on <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ec 1:13</reference>). <div eID="gen12464" type="x-p"/>
entries.51a9f67e14eb71420d97003f51ca0759d2f4f998: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8030"/><div sID="gen12465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8030"/><hi type="bold">11. his time--</hi>that is, in its proper season (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>), opposed to worldlings putting earthly pursuits out of their proper time and place (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.9">Ec 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set the world in their heart--</hi>given them capacities to understand the world of nature as reflecting God's wisdom in its beautiful order and times (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.19">Ro 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). "Everything" answers to "world," in the parallelism.<div eID="gen12466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that--</hi>that is, but in such a manner that man only sees a portion, not the whole "from beginning to end" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Re 15:4</reference>). Parkhurst, for "world," translates: "Yet He hath put obscurity in the midst of them," literally, "a secret," so man's mental dimness of sight as to the full mystery of God's works. So Holden and Weiss. This incapacity for "finding out" (comprehending) God's work is chiefly the fruit of the fall. The worldling ever since, not knowing God's time and order, labors in vain, because out of time and place. <div eID="gen12467" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fd2492a3ee4d3ccc8baa384ddd3769276a5cf1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8031"/><div sID="gen12468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8031"/><hi type="bold">12. in them--</hi>in God's works (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>), as far as relates to man's duty. Man cannot fully comprehend them, but he ought joyfully to receive ("rejoice in") God's gifts, and "do good" with them to himself and to others. This is never out of season (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Ga 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.10">10</reference>). Not sensual joy and self-indulgence (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">Php 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.16">Jas 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen12468" type="x-p"/>
entries.8820766deffecfb2b4fd3a9b4f41d01d31aeb10b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8032"/><div sID="gen12469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8032"/>13. Literally, "And also as to every man who eats ... this is the gift of God" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>). When received as God's gifts, and to God's glory, the good things of life are enjoyed in their due time and order (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">Ac 2:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1Co 10:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen12469" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ecc0f52e726c6574e06f61138d601bf5713f1de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8033"/><div sID="gen12470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8033"/>14. (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.12">1Sa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.34">Psa 89:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.35">Mt 24:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen12470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>as opposed to man's perishing labors (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.15-Eccl.2.18">Ec 2:15-18</reference>).<div eID="gen12471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">any thing taken from it--</hi>opposed to man's "crooked and wanting" works (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ec 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.13">7:13</reference>). The event of man's labors depends wholly on God's immutable purpose. Man's part, therefore, is to do and enjoy every earthly thing in its proper season (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">13</reference>), not setting aside God's order, but observing deep reverence towards God; for the mysteriousness and unchangeableness of God's purposes are designed to lead "man to fear before Him." Man knows not the event of each act: otherwise he would think himself independent of God. <div eID="gen12472" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b1d8636266d2aa006d9f8def1730638f628e6fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8034"/><div sID="gen12473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8034"/>15. Resumption of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>. Whatever changes there be, the succession of events is ordered by God's "everlasting" laws (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Ec 3:14</reference>), and returns in a fixed cycle.<div eID="gen12473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">requireth that ... past--</hi>After many changes, God's law requires the return of the same cycle of events, as in the past, literally, "that which is driven on." The Septuagint and Syriac translate: "God requireth (that is, avengeth) the persecuted man"; a transition to <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">17</reference>. The parallel clauses of the verse support English Version. <div eID="gen12474" type="x-p"/>
entries.adab9f04923382abb87abed61b5243276608ccb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8035"/><div sID="gen12475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8035"/>16. Here a difficulty is suggested. If God "requires" events to move in their perpetual cycle, why are the wicked allowed to deal unrighteously in the place where injustice ought least of all to be; namely, "the place of judgment" (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>)? <div eID="gen12475" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a4ffe270b4cf1aaaa24085362433c1b8074ceaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8036"/><div sID="gen12476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8036"/>17. Solution of it. There is a coming judgment in which God will vindicate His righteous ways. The sinner's "time" of his unrighteous "work" is short. God also has His "time" and "work" of judgment; and, meanwhile, is overruling, for good at last, what seems now dark. Man cannot now "find out" the plan of God's ways (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference>). If judgment instantly followed every sin, there would be no scope for free will, faith, and perseverance of saints in spite of difficulties. The previous darkness will make the light at last the more glorious.<div eID="gen12476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.3.17-Job.3.19">Job 3:17-19</reference>) in eternity, in the presence of the Divine Judge, opposed to the "there," in the human place of judgment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>): so "from thence" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>). <div eID="gen12477" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a126a9e837192c3f7556d3b06c61221d72f48bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8037"/><div sID="gen12478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8037"/><hi type="bold">18. estate--</hi>The estate of fallen man is so ordered (these wrongs are permitted), that God might "manifest," that is, thereby prove them, and that they might themselves see their mortal frailty, like that of the beasts.<div eID="gen12478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons of men--</hi>rather, "sons of Adam," a phrase used for "fallen men." The toleration of injustice until the judgment is designed to "manifest" men's characters in their fallen state, to see whether the oppressed will bear themselves aright amidst their wrongs, knowing that the time is short, and there is a coming judgment. The oppressed share in death, but the comparison to "beasts" applies especially to the ungodly oppressors (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">20</reference>). They too need to be "manifested" ("proved"), whether, considering that they must soon die as the "beasts," and fearing the judgment to come, they will repent (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Da 4:27</reference>). <div eID="gen12479" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b6cda22c6a084483c93cd80079915721bfe3c3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8038"/><div sID="gen12480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8038"/>19. Literally, "For the sons of men (Adam) are a mere chance, as also the beast is a mere chance." These words can only be the sentiments of the skeptical oppressors. God's delay in judgment gives scope for the "manifestation" of their infidelity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>,<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">4</reference>). They are "brute beasts," morally (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18">Ec 3:18</reference>; Jude 10); and they end by maintaining that man, physically, has no pre-eminence over the beast, both alike being "fortuities." Probably this was the language of Solomon himself in his apostasy. He answers it in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Ec 3:21</reference>. If <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">Ec 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.20">20</reference> be his words, they express only that as regards liability to death, excluding the future judgment, as the skeptic oppressors do, man is on a level with the beast. Life is "vanity," if regarded independently of religion. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Ec 3:21</reference> points out the vast difference between them in respect to the future destiny; also (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>) beasts have no "judgment" to come.<div eID="gen12480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breath--</hi>vitality. <div eID="gen12481" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c12df667168b0dd4bf6efe179c5ea39671a317f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8039"/><div sID="gen12482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8039"/><hi type="bold">21. Who knoweth--</hi>Not doubt of the destination of man's spirit (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Ec 12:7</reference>); but "how few, by reason of the outward mortality to which man is as liable as the beast and which is the ground of the skeptic's argument, comprehend the wide difference between man and the beast" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Is 53:1</reference>). The Hebrew expresses the difference strongly, "The spirit of man that ascends, it belongeth to on high; but the spirit of the beast that descends, it belongeth to below, even to the earth." Their destinations and proper element differ utterly [Weiss]. <div eID="gen12482" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f7c37c7b1f58fcce5b1e30eabd2c3b0d4740c30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8040"/><div sID="gen12483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8040"/>22. (Compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>). Inculcating a thankful enjoyment of God's gifts, and a cheerful discharge of man's duties, founded on fear of God; not as the sensualist (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>); not as the anxious money-seeker (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.23">Ec 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10-2Cor.5.17">5:10-17</reference>).<div eID="gen12483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his portion--</hi>in the present life. If it were made his main portion, it would be "vanity" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ec 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Lu 16:25</reference>).<div eID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for who, &c.--</hi>Our ignorance as to the future, which is God's "time" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>), should lead us to use the present time in the best sense and leave the future to His infinite wisdom (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.20">Mt 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31-Matt.25.34">25, 31-34</reference>). <chapter eID="Eccl.3"/>

entries.9aca5962f16e6da98c798cf69c8958c51ddae253: <div eID="gen25306" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25307" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25308" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25308" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25307" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25309" type="x-p"/> Every thing has its time and season, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.1-Ecc.3.8">Ecc 3:1-8</reference>. Men are exercised with labor, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.9">Ecc 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.10">Ecc 3:10</reference>. Every thing is beautiful in its season, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.11">Ecc 3:11</reference>. Men should enjoy thankfully the gifts of God, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.12">Ecc 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.13">Ecc 3:13</reference>. What God does is for ever, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.14">Ecc 3:14</reference>. There is nothing new, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.15">Ecc 3:15</reference>. The corruption of judgment; but the judgments of God are right, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.16">Ecc 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.17">Ecc 3:17</reference>. Man is brutish, and men and brutes die in like manner, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.18-Ecc.3.21">Ecc 3:18-21</reference>. Man may enjoy the fruit of his own labors, <reference osisRef="Ecc.3.22">Ecc 3:22</reference>. <div eID="gen25309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose - Two general remarks may be made on the first eight verses of this chapter. <div eID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> 1. God by his providence governs the world, and has determined particular things and operations to particular times. In those times such things may be done with propriety and success; but if we neglect the appointed seasons, we sin against this providence, and become the authors of our own distresses. <div eID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25313" type="x-p"/> 2. God has given to man that portion of duration called Time; the space in which all the operations of nature, of animals, and intellectual beings, are carried on; but while nature is steady in its course, and animals faithful to their instincts, man devotes it to a great variety of purposes; but very frequently to that for which God never made time, space, or opportunity. And all we can say, when an evil deed is done, is, there was a time in which it was done, though God never made it for that purpose. <div eID="gen25313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> To say any farther on this subject is needless, as the words themselves give in general their own meaning. The Jews, it is true, see in these times and seasons all the events of their own nation, from the birth of Abraham to the present times; and as to fathers and their followers, they see all the events and states of the Christian Church in them! <div eID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25315" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark, that in all this list there are but two things which may be said to be done generally by the disposal of God, and in which men can have but little influence: the time of birth, and the time of death. But all the others are left to the option of man, though God continues to overrule them by his providence. The following paraphrase will explain all that is necessary to be generally understood: -
entries.24e96288a77ad1ecad26bb982be079d132353526: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> A time to be born, and a time to die - plant - "As in its mother's womb the embryo lies <div eID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25317" type="x-p"/> A space determined; to full growth arrived, <div eID="gen25317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25318" type="x-p"/> From its dark prison bursts, and sees the light; <div eID="gen25318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25319" type="x-p"/> So is the period fix'd when man shall drop <div eID="gen25319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25320" type="x-p"/> Into the grave - A time there is to plant, <div eID="gen25320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25321" type="x-p"/> And sow; another time to pluck and reap. <div eID="gen25321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25322" type="x-p"/> Even nations have their destined rise and fall: <div eID="gen25322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25323" type="x-p"/> Awhile they thrive; and for destruction ripe, <div eID="gen25323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25324" type="x-p"/> When grown, are rooted up like wither'd plants."
entries.e499d095591cacad690649977f41ade1440f9789: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25325" type="x-p"/> A time to kill, - heal, - break down, - build up - "The healing art, when out of season used, <div eID="gen25325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25326" type="x-p"/> Pernicious proves, and serves to hasten death. <div eID="gen25326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25327" type="x-p"/> But timely medicines drooping nature raise, <div eID="gen25327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25328" type="x-p"/> And health restore - Now, Justice wields her sword <div eID="gen25328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25329" type="x-p"/> With wholesome rigour, nor the offender spares: <div eID="gen25329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25330" type="x-p"/> But Mercy now is more expedient found. <div eID="gen25330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25331" type="x-p"/> On crazy fabrics ill-timed cost bestow'd <div eID="gen25331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25332" type="x-p"/> No purpose answers, when discretion bids <div eID="gen25332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25333" type="x-p"/> To pull them down, and wait a season fit <div eID="gen25333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25334" type="x-p"/> To build anew."
entries.2fef27d745d334ddbeedb73a51205a75058fefa5: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25335" type="x-p"/> A time to weep, - laugh, - mourn, - dance - - "When private griefs affect <div eID="gen25335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25336" type="x-p"/> The heart, our tears with decent sorrow flow; <div eID="gen25336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25337" type="x-p"/> Nor less becoming, when the public mourns, <div eID="gen25337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25338" type="x-p"/> To vent the deepest sighs. But all around <div eID="gen25338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25339" type="x-p"/> When things a smiling aspect bear, our souls <div eID="gen25339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25340" type="x-p"/> May well exult; 'tis then a time for joy."
entries.278288ca5b5f6c5cd79d36765d27bb9c958d6795: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25341" type="x-p"/> A time to cast away stones, - to gather stones, - to embrace, - to refrain - "One while domestic cares abortive prove, <div eID="gen25341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25342" type="x-p"/> And then successful. Nature now invites <div eID="gen25342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25343" type="x-p"/> Connubial pleasures: but, when languid grown, <div eID="gen25343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25344" type="x-p"/> No less rejects."
entries.f779bff0d0d347d4e8c4e24aec57ba38e88cd4e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25345" type="x-p"/> A time to get, - to lose, - to keep, - to cast away - - "Commerce produces wealth, <div eID="gen25345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25346" type="x-p"/> Whilst time of gaining lasts; from every point <div eID="gen25346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25347" type="x-p"/> Blow prosperous gales. Now heaven begins to lower, <div eID="gen25347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25348" type="x-p"/> And all our hopes are blasted. Prudence bids, <div eID="gen25348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25349" type="x-p"/> One while, our treasure to reserve, and then <div eID="gen25349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25350" type="x-p"/> With liberal hand to scatter wide. How oft <div eID="gen25350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25351" type="x-p"/> In raging storms, the owner wisely casts <div eID="gen25351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25352" type="x-p"/> Into the deep his precious merchandise, <div eID="gen25352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25353" type="x-p"/> To save the foundering bark!
entries.137bb654b80b35646d438d7ad055b638649e83fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25354" type="x-p"/> A time to rend, - sew, - keep silence, - speak - - "Intestine broils <div eID="gen25354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25355" type="x-p"/> And factions rend a state: at length the breach <div eID="gen25355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25356" type="x-p"/> Is heal'd, and rest ensues.
